1:
What the wars are is the first question, and the answers run from armies to lawsuits. Clarke takes them literally, citing Josephus for the insurrections the Jews raised against the Romans under pretence of defending their religion, and the factions that massacred and plundered each other; the Christians of the time, he adds, had neither the power nor the political consequence to raise contentions at all. Henry agrees the Jews were a seditious people whom the corrupt Christians addressed here had joined, and draws the moral that what is sheltered under a specious pretence of zeal for God often comes from pride, malice, covetousness, ambition and revenge. Barnes prefers domestic broils and the strifes of sects and parties, into which converts were in great danger of being drawn. Gill canvasses national wars, theological disputes, and lawsuits brought by the rich to oppress the poor, before settling on quarrels about honours and riches. Calvin denies the literal sense outright: the language is highly metaphorical, the military terms standing for inward lusts whose expedition was mustered in the heart.

On the cause there is no dispute. Robertson distinguishes the two nouns, the chronic campaign and the separate battles, so that the whole ground is covered; he closes drily that modern church disturbances are old enough in practice. Ellicott quotes Bishop Moberly's figure of desires posted and picketed all over us like soldiers in the devil's army, hoping to win our members back to an allegiance renounced in baptism. Wesley marks the members as the first seat of the war, whence proceeds the war of man with man, king with king, nation with nation. Barnes generalises: the same spirit that leads to a brawl in the street prompted the conquests of Alexander, Caesar and Napoleon, and if true religion existed among all men there would be no more war.

Two voices press it further. Barnes turns the comparison into an indictment: to steal a horse makes a thief and to fire a dwelling an arsonist, but to plunder kingdoms and wrap cities in flames makes an illustrious conqueror, so that one name is enrolled among felons and the other sent down to future times as immortal, though the all-discerning eye may see no difference but in magnitude. Calvin says the soul indulging wicked lust is insatiable, since were the world given to such a man he would wish other worlds created for him, and quotes Horace that the tyrants of Sicily found no torment greater than envy.

The verb in the second verse divides them sharply. Calvin doubts not that we ought to read ye envy rather than ye kill, since to kill does in no way suit the context, and explains the order as the scriptural habit of naming the greater evil first: ye kill because ye envy, envy being murder in the sight of God. Barnes answers that the correct reading is undoubtedly ye kill, that the substitution rests on no manuscript authority and was adopted by Erasmus, Luther and Beza from conjecture, and takes the sense to be a murderous disposition rather than murder committed. Wesley reaches Calvin's meaning without touching the text, since he that hateth his brother is a murderer. Robertson solves it by punctuation, putting a full stop after ye kill so that a second situation begins, ye covet and cannot obtain and so fight and war, which avoids the anticlimax; he reports Mayor's alternative, a hendiadys, ye murderously envy.

On the closing clause the note is practical. Clarke says they get no especial blessing as their fathers did because they do not pray, worldly good being their god. Wesley puts it shortest: a man full of evil desire, of envy or hatred, cannot pray. Henry warns that when we speed not in prayer it is because we ask amiss, for unbelieving and cold desires beg denials.
3:
On praying and not receiving, Barnes is the most uncomfortable. It is not uncommon for men who go to war to pray, or to procure a chaplain to pray for them; the covetous and the quarrelsome pray, keep a form of worship in their families, and ask success in engagements founded on covetousness. When such prayers fail, he says, that is no evidence God does not hear prayer but that the objects or motives were improper; and nowhere is deception more likely to creep in than when we ask for success in our worldly employments. Calvin puts the charge more shortly: they wished to make God the minister of their own lusts, set no bounds to their wishes, and asked what a man conscious of what is right ought to be ashamed of. Pliny somewhere ridicules the impudence of men who so wickedly abuse the ears of God, he recalls, and it is less tolerable in Christians, who have the rule of prayer from their heavenly Master.

Robertson notes that the middle voice does make sense here, ye ask for yourselves, and that the verb behind spend is the one used of squandering; God does not hear prayers like this. Clarke glosses the phrase as asking evilly, calls the idiom Jewish, and reports that the rabbis have many observations on asking improperly. He offers a particular occasion too: some think the prayer meant was for the conversion of the heathen, on the failure of which the petitioners thought it lawful to extirpate them and possess their goods.

The address in the next verse is a textual battlefield, and the witnesses contradict each other. Ellicott says flatly that the received text is wrong and it should read ye adulteresses alone; Robertson agrees that ye adulterers is spurious and belongs to the Syrian text only. But Clarke reports that the feminine is the word wanting, absent from the Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian and Vulgate and from one copy of the Old Latin, and Gill likewise notes the Vulgate, Syriac and Ethiopic leaving out adulteresses. The same versions are cited on both sides for opposite omissions.

Whether the charge is literal divides them further. Calvin says those who take the words literally do not sufficiently observe the context, since the writer goes on speaking of the lusts that entangle men with the world, and the marriage God forms with us is frequent in Scripture. Gill, Barnes, Ellicott and Wesley all read it figuratively, of a broken covenant, Ellicott gathering the passages where God speaks so of Israel and adding the chaste virgin espoused to Christ. Clarke leans that way but will not close the door, allowing that perhaps something more than spiritual adultery is intended. Robertson thinks the literal view probably more in harmony with the language just before, in which case the address may take in more than Christians.

On the friendship of the world the definitions converge. Barnes takes the world for the community rather than the physical creation, and makes the friendship consist in setting the heart on its maxims and ends with the same spirit as those who make no pretence of religion; the test is whether we feel more pain at failing to win the world's applause than at having lost the enjoyment of religion. Ellicott denies any middle ground, since there cannot be a passive condition to the faith of Christ and good and evil divide the land too sharply for a halting-place; renunciation is the earliest severance, not a forsaking of the world when tired of its delights. Calvin measures it: as much as any one inclines to the world, so much he alienates himself from God. Robertson notes that the verb rendered maketh himself is passive, is constituted or rendered. Clarke ends bluntly, that when the world gets into the church the church becomes a painted sepulchre, its spiritual vitality extinct.
5:
No verse here has puzzled the commentators more, and they say so. Barnes reports that few passages have given expositors more perplexity, since no such words stand in the older books, and lists the escapes attempted: a spurious clause begun as a marginal gloss, an apocryphal book, the general spirit rather than any particular place, or no quotation at all but two questions. He rejects them all, since the formula is one of citation and the term for Scripture is never applied to an apocryphal book, and settles on a fifth: the writer had no particular passage in his eye but condensed into his own words a truth taught everywhere, that the soul is inclined to envy. Clarke calls the verse exceedingly obscure, lists four candidate texts, admits none has the precise words, and gives up: there is not a critic in Europe who has considered the passage and not been puzzled by it, and he leaves his paraphrase as the best he can do, not asserting he has hit the meaning.

Robertson agrees no passage is precisely like it, passes on the description of them as a poetical rendering of the second commandment, and floats a further possibility, that the citation points forward to the proverb quoted next, everything between being parenthesis; there is no way, he says, to decide positively. Ellicott is unbothered: surely the substance sufficed without a slavish adherence to the form. Calvin cuts the knot: nothing hinders the reference from being to what has already been said, that the friendship of the world is adverse to God, a truth occurring everywhere in Scripture. Gill records that some looked in the New Testament, some in an apocryphal book.

Whose spirit is meant divides them as sharply. Barnes takes it of our own disposition by nature, and dismisses the alternative, since making it the Holy Spirit forces the rendering into lusting against envy, which the Greek will not well bear. Clarke takes precisely that rejected sense, holding the verse should be read contrary to the received translation, since every genuine Christian is a habitation of the Holy Ghost and that Spirit excites strong desires against envy; a man must not suppose himself a Christian if he has an envious heart. Calvin also reads the Spirit of God and makes the sentence a question, so that the argument runs from the contrary: envy proves malignity, the Spirit proves himself bountiful by the affluence of his blessings, and nothing is more repugnant to his nature. He judges the other explanation, that the Spirit lusts against envy, too harsh and forced. Ellicott offers a jealous sense, the Spirit dwelling in us regarding us as his own, and notes that a varied punctuation turns the clause into a second question. Robertson thinks the Spirit the likelier subject, the verb a yearning after in the good sense.

The next verse is the resolution. Robertson asks greater than what, and answers, greater grace in view of the greater requirement. Ellicott makes it flow from the indwelling, the giver of all good gifts adding to the wasted treasure. Barnes reads it as the writer's own declaration rather than a continuation of the quotation, struck that not all are under the influence of envy and that to some a higher favour is given. On the proverb that follows, Ellicott notes it is an exact quotation from the Greek version except that God stands for Lord, and seems to have been a common saying, a maxim of the wise become a law of life. Robertson and Clarke both gloss the verb as military, God ranging himself in battle array against the proud. Barnes catalogues how providence and the plan of salvation are contrived to humble: the reverses that empty the splendid mansion, the sickness that takes away beauty and strength, the grave, and a Saviour so despised that no feature of the plan can foster pride.
7:
Robertson counts ten aorist imperatives in these four verses and hears urgency in every one; the first is a military word, to range oneself under, the second to take a stand against. Calvin explains the connecting particle: since the Spirit is bountiful in increasing his gifts, we ought to lay aside envy and submit, and the submission asked is humility rather than obedience in general, since the Spirit rests on the humble. Gill applies it to worldly things, that a man should leave God to choose his inheritance for him, since by striving he adds nothing to his substance, any more than a cubit to his stature. Ellicott finds here the hardest advice of all, submission being hardest to a man reliant on himself, and then turns that self-reliance into a virtue: here pride may become a stimulant for good, in contest with the evil one.

On the promise that the devil will flee, Calvin raises the objection himself. It seems refuted by daily experience, since the more strenuously a man resists the more fiercely he is urged; Satan acts playfully when he is not in earnest repelled, employs all his strength against those who really resist, and engages another battle as soon as he is beaten in one. The answer is that fleeing here means being put to flight, or routed, so that however often he returns he always departs vanquished. Ellicott quotes the Shepherd of Hermas, that the devil can fight but cannot conquer, and if you withstand him he will flee beaten and ashamed; he takes the verse for another proof of the personality of Satan, which no figure of speech could otherwise interpret. Barnes prefers direct resistance to argument, since no one is safe who yields in the least and none unsafe who does not.

Drawing near is handled tenderly. Clarke notes the delicacy of the expressions: when a soul sets out to seek God, God sets out to meet it. Ellicott brings the father of the prodigal, who beholds us yet a great way off and runs to hasten our return, and answers his own question who may come into the tabernacle: the penitent too, hands and hearts however polluted. Barnes observes we cannot come literally nearer, since God is always round about us, but may in a spiritual sense. Robertson recalls the priests drawing nigh in the sanctuary, and glosses the address to sinners as a reproach meant to startle and sting.

The pairing of hands and hearts is pressed. Barnes takes the hands for the instruments by which we execute what the heart devises, and warns against resting in external reformation. Clarke divides it exactly: as a man is a sinner his hands must be cleansed from wicked works, and as he is double-minded his heart sanctified, sanctification belonging to the heart because of pollution of mind, cleansing to the hands because of sinful acts. He also thinks the address to sinners begins a new appeal and should have started a new verse. On the call to mourn, Calvin distinguishes the salutary sorrow that leads to repentance from the mourning denounced as a curse on those who laugh, addressing men inebriated in mind who exult on the verge of destruction. Clarke infers from the vocabulary of laughter and joy that a dissolute life is meant, and doubts such words could have been addressed to a church few in number, without wealth, and persecuted. Ellicott makes wretchedness, sorrow and tears the three steps of the homeward way, and asks for the remorseful anguish of a Peter and not a Judas. Robertson notes that the word for heaviness describes the hanging down of the eyes, like the publican's. On the last verse Barnes says the humbling is to be in God's sight because our sins are chiefly against him, and Gill lists the acknowledgment of meanness and unworthiness that Abraham, Job and the publican made.
11:
The prohibition is defined before it is argued. Henry takes the Greek to cover anything that may hurt another, so that we must not speak evil things of others though they be true, unless there be some necessary occasion; our lips must be guided by the law of kindness as well as by truth, and where we cannot speak well we had better say nothing. Robertson glosses it as harsh words about the absent, the writer returning to the subject of the tongue. Gill lists the forms it takes, raising false reports, aggravating failings, depreciating characters, and calls it barbarous and unnatural in saints, whatever it be in the men of the world. Clarke reports the rabbinic maxim that no one speaks evil of his brother without denying God and becoming an atheist, and traces detraction to the devil, whose original crime was to calumniate God in Eden, insinuating the tree was forbidden out of envy. Ellicott defines the fault as setting up our own tribunals, in which we are at once prosecutor, witness, law, lawgiver and judge; rebuke itself is not condemned, John the Baptist being the example against that.

What law is judged is the harder question. Barnes takes it for the law of Christ, elsewhere called the law of liberty, and reads it against a particular quarrel: those who held the Mosaic ceremonies still binding condemned brethren who did not keep them, and so condemned the law that had released men from that servitude. Not a few of the harsh judgments one sort of religionist passes on another, he adds, are in fact judgments on the laws of Christ, since we set up our own interpretations and judge men for not complying. Henry reads it the same way: those who censure a brother over things the law has left indifferent censure the law itself. Calvin brings in the same comparison from Paul about meats, and finds beneath it a disease innate in human nature, that every one would have all others live according to his own fancy; so much is taken from the law as a man claims of authority over his brethren. Robertson puts it shortly: the tone of superiority to law is what is condemned, and we cannot select the laws we obey unless some contravene God's law and our conscience.

Clarke dissents from that reading. He grants that most critics take the law for the gospel and the lawgiver for Christ, but this is not clear to him: he believes the Jewish law is meant and the lawgiver God Almighty, since from the closest examination of the epistle he finds but few references to Christ or his gospel, the writer keeping his Jewish creed and maxims constantly in view. Gill declines the choice and applies the character to the Father, who gave Israel the law, and to the Son, lawgiver in his own house, who gave the new commandment of love that detraction most apparently breaks. Barnes turns his reading into a principle of church polity: no laws bind the conscience but those Christ has ordained, though the tendency everywhere has been to enact the laws of synods and councils and hold Christians bound to observe them.

A variant is reported in the same clause. Clarke notes that and judge is added by two of the great copies and some thirty others, and by the Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopic and Vulgate, and on that evidence was received into the text by Griesbach; Gill notes the same addition in the Alexandrian copy. On the closing question the voices sharpen. Ellicott makes God the fountain of law as a king is of honour, all judgment being delegated from him, and quotes Bengel that it is not our part to judge since we cannot carry out our sentence. Robertson notes the emphatic pronoun in the rhetorical question. Wesley answers it in four words: a poor, dying worm.
13:
The opening call is read as a summons to attention. Barnes calls it a phrase designed to arrest notice, implying that what follows is wrong; Clarke matches it to the Hebrew word for come, and Robertson notes the interjection standing with a plural verb. The scene itself is drawn from trade. Barnes quotes a description of the practice as still common in the East, the merchant carrying the products of one place to a distant city, staying until his goods are sold and others bought for a further market, and repeating this for years until he can return home prosperous. Clarke says the Jews traded so from city to city with their goods on camels, to Tyre and Sidon, to Ephesus, Corinth and Rome, and that this itinerant mercantile life is meant. Robertson finds the same picture in the verb, which belongs to the man who goes in and gets the trade, and adds Mayor's touch that the speaker would be pointing at the city on a map as he made the proposal.

Clarke supports the rebuke from a rabbinic story. Rabbi Simeon, present at a circumcision, stayed to the entertainment, where the father brought out wine seven years old and said that with it he would go on celebrating his new son's birth for a long time. Leaving at midnight, Simeon met the angel of death walking up and down, and asked why he wandered so. I slay those persons, came the answer, who say we will do this or that and think not how soon death may overpower them; the man with whom thou hast supped shall die within thirty days.

Calvin alone qualifies the rebuke. He insists that the form of speaking is not reproved but the arrogance of mind behind it, since even the godly, who know their steps are guided, may say without any qualifying clause that they will do this or that; the servants of God everywhere in Scripture speak unconditionally of future things, and no scruple ought to be entertained as though it were a sin to omit the clause, though the practice of using it deserves careful attention. What is reproved is the stupidity of men who claimed a whole year while they had not a single moment in their own power, and promised themselves the gain that was far off while they had no possession of what lay before their feet.

On the figure of the vapour the voices differ over its subject. Ellicott makes the thrust sharper than the received version allows: not merely life is the vapour, which is confessedly a breath, but ye yourselves and all belonging to you; and he hears a play on words in the antithesis of appearing and vanishing. Barnes keeps to the life, and presses the impossibility of building on it — who can calculate on the permanence of a vapour, or build solid hopes on a mist? He takes the word for the exhalation that lies on the mountain side and is dissipated by the rising sun leaving no trace, and observes that the house a man has built and the book he has written remain a little while, but the life is gone. Gill puts the same practically, that no man can secure a day, an hour, or a moment.

The classical parallels are gathered on both sides. Barnes says the classic writings abound with beautiful expressions on the uncertainty of the future, some almost precisely in these words, and names Anacreon, Euripides, Menander, Seneca and Horace. Clarke adds Pliny asking what is so circumscribed, so short, as the longest life of man, then sets the son of Sirach on the green leaves of a thick tree, some falling and some growing, beside Homer's generations of leaves in Pope's version, and asks whether the one borrowed from the other.
15:
The prescribed words are guarded against becoming a formula. Barnes says the meaning is not that we ought always to say it in so many words, since that might become a mere ostentatious form, offensive by constant unmeaning repetition, but that we should recognise our dependence and form all our plans with reference to God's will. Robertson agrees, calling it the proper attitude of mind and not something to be uttered always in words like a charm; he notes the same formula was common among the ancient heathen and is so among Arabs today. Calvin finds a twofold condition, if we live so long and if the Lord will, so that living and doing alike depend on him, and specifies that the will meant is not the one expressed in the law but the counsel by which God governs all things. Ellicott presses the tense, the condition being completed action on God's part, if the Lord have willed it; and he distinguishes this from fatalism even in its best form, since the sovereignty of God is acknowledged together with the existence of man's free will.

Clarke brings two illustrations, one from either side of the ancient world. The rabbis tell of a man who said that tomorrow he would sit with his bride in his chamber and rejoice with her; when bystanders added, if the Lord will, he answered that whether the Lord willed or not he would do it. He did go in with his bride that night, and both of them died before morning. Beside this Clarke sets a passage of Lucian he read as a schoolboy, in which a man invited to supper the next day said he would certainly come, and while he was still speaking a tile fell from a roof and killed him, so that the speaker laughs at him for not keeping his engagement. We should learn even from our enemies, Clarke says, and warns the Christian not to let a heathen buffoon laugh him out of countenance.

The boasting that follows is defined narrowly. Ellicott notes the word is the one rendered the pride of life elsewhere, meaning braggart boastfulness and not the innocent gladness of living; it is the trust of the ungodly who say no harm shall happen to them, and the mistaken confidence of even godly men, like Job expecting to die in his nest before the Almighty instructed him by trouble and loss. Robertson calls it an old word for braggart talk, common in Aristophanes, and distinguishes the glorying, good if for Christ and bad if for self. Barnes locates the fault in a reliance on one's own skill and sagacity, plans laid as if failure were impossible and life secure from the numberless casualties that may defeat them. Clarke hears in it men exulting that they are free from the trammels of superstition and can live independently of God, and quotes an old English book on those who thank God for their unholiness, that they had best go ring the bells for joy that they shall never see God. Calvin says what is condemned is more than a passing speech: they did not openly set themselves above God, but their minds were inebriated with vanity so as to disregard him.

The closing maxim is read as the conclusion of the whole. Calvin anticipates the contemptuous answer that such warnings tell men only what they already know, and turns it against them, since they sinned the more grievously in sinning not through ignorance but through contempt. Barnes takes the proposition as general but meant chiefly of the plans just described, and quotes the principle Cotton Mather adopted, that the ability to do good in any case imposes an obligation to do it. Gill extends it further still, to all the good things the epistle has urged and all the evils it has warned against.
